The reviewed literature and related studies show that artificial intelligence and educational information systems are becoming important tools in improving assessment practices, academic monitoring, and decision-making in higher education. Several sources emphasized that AI, particularly large language models, can assist in feedback generation, scoring, content preparation, and interpretation of academic data. However, the studies also show that AI models should be evaluated first before being used in an actual system
because their outputs may differ in relevance, accuracy, consistency, and response time depending on the task, prompt, data, and educational context.

The findings also highlight the importance of integrating AI into educational systems in a guided and responsible way. Existing studies on AI-supported platforms, learning management systems, automated feedback tools, and adaptive learning environments show that AI can help teachers process academic information and produce structured learning-related outputs. This is relevant to AIssessment because the system does not use AI as a separate tool. Instead, the identified AI model is integrated into the student performance monitoring workflow to generate draft formative and summative report content based on students’ most learned and least learned skills.

Another important pattern from the reviewed works is the need to evaluate AI-generated academic outputs alongside teacher-generated outputs. Related studies showed that AI-generated feedback and content can be fast, organized, and useful, but teacher-generated outputs remain important because of human judgment, contextual understanding, instructional experience, and professional responsibility. This supports the direction of AIssessment, where AI-generated report content is not treated as final output. Instead, it will be compared with teacher-generated report content in terms of tim
, while still allowing instructors to review and finalize the generated report content.

The reviewed sources also emphasize that system acceptability plays an important role in the success of educational technologies. Studies on technology acceptance, student information systems, e-assessment platforms, and AI-powered educational tools show that users are more likely to accept a system when they find it useful, easy to use,

understandable, trustworthy, and relevant to their tasks. This is important for AIssessment because the system will be used by different intended users, including the Super Admin, Admin/Dean, Department Chair, Instructor, and Student. For the system to be accepted, it must support their actual responsibilities in
academic setup, class management, assessment management, student performance monitoring, and report preparation.

Despite the contributions of existing studies, several limitations remain evident. Many systems and studies focus only on selected parts of the process, such as AI model evaluation, automated feedback, student information management, teacher-AI feedback comparison, or system acceptability. However, few address these needs in one integrated platform. This shows the need for a system that combines class management, assessment management, assessment submissions, student performance monitoring, role-based academic access, and AI-assisted formative and summative report content generation within a single web-based environment.

Based on these findings, the researchers identified the need to develop AIssessment: An AI-Based Student Performance Monitoring System for Pangasinan State University. The proposed system aims to address the identified gaps by providing a web-based platform that supports academic setup, class management, assessment management, performance monitoring, and AI-assisted report content generation. Through the integration of an evaluated AI model and teacher-reviewed report output, AIssessment seeks to provide a more organized, responsible, and acceptable approach to student performance monitoring within the university.

This section presents the technical structure of AIssessment as the proposed system developed for Pangasinan State University. The project is designed as an AI-based student performance monitoring system that organizes class records, assessments, student submissions, performance results, and formative and summative reports in one web-based platform. Its technical design supports academic users by making assessment-related records easier to manage while assisting instructors in preparing report content based on students’ most learned and least learned skills.

AIssessment is designed to support the academic monitoring process through user management, class management, assessment handling, student submissions, performance monitoring, and AI-assisted report generation. Instead of relying on manual records or separate files, the system provides a structured platform where assessment data and performance information can be managed more efficiently.
The system has five user levels: Super Admin, Admin/Dean, Department Chair, Instructor, and Student.

The Super Admin manages system-wide academic setup, including colleges, departments, programs, subjects, student accounts, and high-level system access, such as the assignment or removal of Admin/Dean and Department Chair designations.
The Admin/Dean manages departments, programs, instructors, and student accounts within the assigned college.

The Department Chair manages instructors and student accounts within the assigned department and its related programs and can access finalized reports only from instructors under the assigned department.

The Instructor handles the main academic process in the system. Instructors can create classes, import student rosters, approve student join requests, prepare assessments, publish assessments to specific classes, monitor student results, and generate formative and summative reports. When a student roster is imported, the system matches the student numbers with existing student records and adds the matched students to the class. This setup allows the system to support flexible class arrangements without depending only on fixed sections.

For assessment management, instructors create assessments under a specific subject. These assessments may be reused across different classes that handle the same subject, but they only become available to students once published or assigned to a particular class. This allows instructors to set class-specific options such as availability period, due date, attempt limit, score visibility, answer visibility, item shuffling, choice shuffling, and warning limit.
The Student uses the system to access enrolled classes, take assigned assessments, submit answers, and view scores or released results
depending on the instructor’s settings. After submission, the system records the student’s answers and uses the results to compute scores and provide class-based performance information.

AIssessment also includes score release and answer visibility controls. Through these settings, instructors can decide whether students may only view their scores or also review their submitted answers and the correct answers after an assessment has closed.
This helps instructors manage assessment review properly, especially when the same assessment may still be used in other classes.

Another important feature of the system is AI-assisted report generation. Based on student assessment results, the system helps generate draft formative and summative report content that highlights the most learned and least learned skills of students. The generated content is not treated as final output; instructors can review, edit, and finalize it before saving the report.

Overall, the technical flow of AIssessment begins with user and academic setup, followed by class creation, student roster import, assessment preparation, assessment publishing, student submission, performance monitoring, and report generation. This flow allows the system to support a more organized
and technology-assisted approach to student performance monitoring.

The study uses researcher-made instruments to gather data needed for the analysis, development, integration, and evaluation of AIssessment: An AI-Based Student Performance Monitoring System for Pangasinan State University. Observation, document analysis, and interviews are used to understand the existing student performance monitoring process, identify report requirements, and determine user needs, while evaluation instruments are used to assess candidate AI models, compare AI-generated and teacher-generated report content, and evaluate system acceptability. Dawadi, Shrestha, and Giri (2021) explained that using multiple data collection methods provides a more comprehensive understanding of a research problem.

Observation is conducted to examine how student performance is currently monitored, recorded, and reviewed. It focuses on identifying the actual workflow used in handling assessment results and preparing reports, as well as the challenges encountered in the process. Chand (2025) noted that observation allows researchers to capture real-world behaviors and contextual factors that may not be fully expressed by participants.

Document analysis is conducted to review existing student performance monitoring records and report formats used by instructors. This includes assessment summaries and formative and summative report templates. This helps determine the required structure and contents for system-generated reports, such as assessment scores, performance indicators,
and learning competencies. Morgan (2022) stated that document analysis helps identify relevant information and requirements reflected in written materials.

Interviews are conducted with selected instructors and academic personnel to gather detailed information regarding their experiences in managing assessments, monitoring student performance, and preparing reports. This also helps identify system requirements and expected features, including class management, assessment handling, result viewing, and report preparation. Xu et al. (2025) explained that interviews are effective in exploring user experiences and needs through in-depth discussion.

For the evaluation phase, evaluation instruments are used to assess candidate AI models using ChatGPT/GPT-based and Claude models. These models are tested using standardized prompts related to assessment analysis and report generation. They are evaluated in terms of relevance, accuracy, and response time to determine the most suitable model for integration into AIssessment. These models are considered due to their application in academic tasks such as grading and evaluating written responses (Bernik, Radošević, and Čep, 2025; Jauhiainen and Guerra, 2024).

The study also compares AI-generated report content with teacher-generated report content in terms of time efficiency and accuracy. In addition, a system acceptability questionnaire is used to evaluate the acceptability of AIssessment among its intended users.

Overall, the use of observation, document analysis, interviews, and evaluation instruments allows the researchers to gather both descriptive and evaluative data needed for the development and evaluation of the system.

A Data Flow Diagram (DFD) is used in system analysis and design to present how data move within a process or system. It shows where information comes from, how it passes through different activities, where records are stored, and what outputs are produced. By using a DFD, the relationship among users, processes, and records becomes cl

The diagram uses standard symbols to represent the main components of the system. Rectangles represent external entities that send or receive data, circles or ovals represent processes that handle the data, open-ended rectangles represent data stores where records are kept, and arrows show the direction of data movement. It illustrates how assessment details, student responses, checked results, performance records, and formative and summative reports are handled in the current manual setup, as well as how these data will be organized more systematically in the proposed system. Through this diagram, the researchers were able to see the main differences between the existing process and the improved process supported by AIssessment.
